meta.subtitle: A cash-generative Classic base funds New Expensify, but revenue is still shrinking and the Street already sits above the price

analystSentiment.commentary: Expensify's Q2'26 10-Q shows a company that has cut its way to cash generation while its top line keeps slipping. Revenue was $33.9M, down 5% year over year, and gross margin fell to 48% from 52% in the same quarter of 2025. Against that, the earnings release reports $6.4 million of free cash flow for the quarter and guides to $12.0 million - $14.0 million for fiscal 2026. The CEO's shareholder letter argues that New Expensify is the growth engine, citing revenue from net new customers up over 250% year over year to over $10 million ARR; the 10-Q itself does not break that business out, so we treat the claim as management's framing rather than a reported figure. At $2.25 the shares sit near the top of the 52-week range of $0.69 – $2.81 and below the consensus target of $2.83. Our probability-weighted value lands close to the current price, so we rate the stock HOLD: the cash flow supports the floor, but there is no reported revenue growth yet to support a re-rating.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Expensify, Inc. sells a cloud-based expense management platform covering corporate cards, bill pay, invoicing and travel booking to individuals, small and midsized businesses and enterprises; it was founded in 2008 and is based in San Francisco. Per the 10-Q MD&A, revenue comes from subscription fees, charged on monthly active members and level of service, plus interchange on the Expensify Card, issued through The Bancorp Bank, N.A. on the Visa network. Cashback paid to cardholders is booked as contra revenue. For the quarter ended June 30, 2026 the MD&A reports an average of 640,000 paid members across an average of 45,700 companies. The company reports a single segment, and FY25 revenue was $142.1M.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: The bull argument is that a profitable but shrinking Classic product is funding a fast-growing New Expensify. The bear argument is that consolidated revenue is still falling and that the FY26E consensus of ~$135.9M bakes in another down year. We sit between them. Free cash flow guidance gives the equity real support, and the Q2 buyback shrank the share count. But paid members are declining, gross margin is compressing as cashback rises, and the stock has already moved from the bottom of its 52-week range to near the top. Until the 10-Q shows the new-customer growth in consolidated revenue, we see the price as roughly fair.

catalysts: Evidence in reported revenue that New Expensify growth is offsetting the Classic drain (see Growth).
Delivery against the fiscal 2026 free cash flow guidance (see Cash flow).
Further share repurchases funded from operating cash flow (see Capital allocation).
risks: Subscription revenue and paid members keep falling as the Classic base drains (see Risks).
Cashback growth on the Expensify Card keeps eroding net revenue and gross margin (see Income statement).
A dual-class structure with a Voting Trust that limits outside holders' influence (see Governance).

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue, net fell 5% in Q2'26 to $33.9M, which the 10-Q MD&A attributes to lower billable activity across the user base and higher contra revenue from Expensify Card cashback, partly offset by higher interchange. Subscription revenue was $30.8 million against $32.9 million a year earlier, while interchange revenue rose to $5.9 million from $5.3 million and the cost of cashback rewards rose to $3.0 million from $2.5 million. In other words, card adoption adds interchange but also adds contra revenue, so the card program does less for net revenue than the interchange line alone suggests. Gross margin fell to 48% from 52%; the MD&A cites higher amortization of capitalized software, partly offset by savings from using AI in place of human agents, and Visa volume incentives that reduce cost of revenue fell to $0.2 million from $0.8 million. Below gross profit the picture improves: total operating expenses fell to 19,251 from 28,915 (in thousands), driven by sales and marketing, which fell to 4,677 from 14,346. The MD&A excerpt is truncated before the sales and marketing discussion, so the filing text available to us does not say why that line fell, and we do not assume it is a run-rate. Net loss narrowed to $3.9 million from $8.8 million, while the earnings release reports non-GAAP net income of $3.4 million and Adjusted EBITDA of $6.6 million; the gap is stock-based compensation, which the company excludes from non-GAAP net income by definition and which was 7,211 (in thousands) in the quarter. Our view is that the cost base has improved faster than revenue, which is a margin story, not a growth story.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: The vendor balance sheet table rounds to $0.1B, which is too coarse to track Expensify's year-to-year changes, and the excerpts we have do not state a quarter-end cash balance. What the data does show is liquidity: the current ratio was 3.30 at FY25 and 3.50 on a trailing basis, and the vendor shows no total debt for FY25. The 10-Q MD&A also notes that other income, which is mostly interest income, fell to 202 from 889 (in thousands) in Q2, consistent with less interest income, though the excerpt does not give the cause. The counter-case to a clean balance sheet is that the Q2 tender and open-market buybacks used cash that would otherwise have earned that interest. On balance we see no solvency question; the balance sheet is a support for the equity, not a driver of it.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the strongest part of the case. FY25 free cash flow was $20.1M, an FCF margin of 14.1%, even as operating margin was -12.7%, and the earnings release reports $8.4 million of cash from operating activities and $6.4 million of free cash flow in Q2'26. Management guides fiscal 2026 free cash flow to $12.0 million - $14.0 million, below the FY25 level. Two caveats temper the picture. One is that the company's free cash flow definition excludes changes in settlement assets and liabilities from the Expensify Card program, so it is not the same as reported operating cash flow less capex. The other is that stock-based compensation, guided at $5.4 to $7.4 million for Q3 2026 and driven by pre-IPO RSUs with about three years of vesting left, is a real cost to holders that free cash flow does not capture. We treat the guidance as credible but declining, which is why it anchors our floor rather than our upside.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing GAAP earnings the stock is loss-making, with a P/E of -14.1x, so earnings multiples rest on forecasts. Consensus FY26E EPS is $0.12 and FY27E EPS is $0.10, which gives a forward P/E of ~22.5x on FY27E and 18.8x on an NTM basis. The vendor does not state whether consensus EPS is GAAP or adjusted; because the company reported a GAAP net loss in Q2'26 alongside positive non-GAAP net income, we read the consensus as closer to the non-GAAP basis, and the forward multiples should be read with that in mind. On sales the stock trades at 1.5x P/S, against consensus revenue that is flat to down through FY27E at $136.1M. A high-teens to low-twenties forward multiple on falling EPS estimates is not cheap for a company with no reported revenue growth. The Street's targets range from $2.50–$3.00, with a consensus of $2.83, and our Base case sits at the low end of that range.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: New Expensify growth shows up in consolidated revenue, paid members stabilize, and the market accepts the CEO's sum-of-the-parts framing; the stock reaches the top of the Street target range at $3.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue tracks consensus of ~$135.9M for FY26E and $136.1M for FY27E, free cash flow lands within the $12.0 million - $14.0 million guide, and the stock holds near the low end of the Street target range at $2.50.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The Classic drain outpaces new-customer growth, which pulls revenue below consensus and free cash flow below the guide; the stock returns to the $1.63 average price the company paid for its open-market repurchases in Q2.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 50% because the consensus path and the free cash flow guide are consistent with each other and with the Q2 run-rate. We put 30% on Bear, more than on Bull, because the Bear driver needs one thing to go wrong, a faster Classic decline, while the Bull driver needs reported revenue to turn and the market to re-rate it. The Bull case at 20% is anchored to the top of the Street range rather than to the CEO's view that each business alone is worth more than today's valuation, which we cannot test with reported figures. The weighted outcome sits close to today's price, which supports HOLD rather than BUY.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Expensify reports a single segment, with FY25 revenue of $142.1M. Within it, the 10-Q MD&A splits revenue sources into subscription fees and Expensify Card interchange, with cashback netted against revenue. The CEO's shareholder letter describes two products, Expensify Classic and New Expensify, that share servers, code, team and customers; the company does not report them as segments, and the letter gives no revenue split between them beyond the net-new-customer ARR figure discussed in Growth.

moatFactors.name: Installed base and workflow integration
moatFactors.body: The MD&A reports over 15 million members added since founding and 1.9 billion expense transactions processed as of June 30, 2026, and the platform exports into third-party systems. That history supports cash flow. But paid members fell 2% year over year in Q2'26, and the MD&A says month-to-month arrangements can be terminated without penalty, so the base offers limited lock-in.

moatFactors.name: Expensify Card economics
moatFactors.body: Interchange revenue rose 12% year over year in Q2'26 and ties customers' spend to the platform. The counter-case is that the program depends on an agreement with The Bancorp Bank, N.A. and on cashback that the 10-Q books as contra revenue, so the card's net contribution is smaller than gross interchange.

moatFactors.name: Pricing and competition
moatFactors.body: The FY25 10-K risk factors list pricing pressure from competition and competitors' feature launches among the drivers of results. With gross margin down to 50.3% in FY25 from 62.4% in FY21, the margin history does not show pricing power.

businessMoat.durability: We see no durable moat today. Expensify's cash generation comes from an installed Classic base that the CEO himself describes as a fixed pool that will naturally drain, and a moat that is shrinking by design is not a moat. A moat could form if New Expensify scales and the card program deepens customer reliance, but neither shows yet in consolidated revenue, which declined in Q2'26.

points: The growth case rests on New Expensify. In the Q2 shareholder letter, the CEO says revenue from net new customers, who have never used Classic, grew by over 250% year over year to over $10 million ARR across over 10,000 new customers. This is a management-defined metric in the earnings release, not a figure reported in the 10-Q, and it is not reconciled to revenue.

The counter-case is the consolidated top line: Q2'26 revenue fell 5%, and FY26E consensus revenue of ~$135.9M implies another down year against FY25. Until New Expensify is large enough to show in reported revenue, the Classic decline dominates.

The Expensify Card is the reported growth line. Interchange revenue rose 12% year over year in Q2'26, but rising cashback means net card contribution grows more slowly, as the income statement section explains.

Product investment continues. The earnings release lists AI-powered workflow agents entering beta, the launch of the Expensify MCP, and 30+ product improvements in Q2. None of these has a disclosed revenue contribution, so we treat them as options rather than inputs to our estimates.

The CEO points to a large untapped market, citing 300 million businesses worldwide, of which he says less than 1% has ever paid for an expense tool. That is the CEO's estimate in the shareholder letter, and the path he describes depends on migrating remaining Classic customers and scaling self-service acquisition.

management.leadership: David Barrett is Founder and CEO and signs the shareholder letter in the Q2'26 earnings release. The letter is candid that Classic is a shrinking base and that the path back to sustained growth depends on migrating remaining Classic customers and accelerating new-customer acquisition. It is also promotional, describing Q2 in glowing terms and arguing each product alone is worth more than the current valuation. We give credit for the candor about Classic and discount the valuation claims, which the reported figures do not yet support.
management.capitalAllocation: In Q2'26 the company launched a modified Dutch auction tender offer for up to $25 million of Class A stock and repurchased 6.1 million shares at $1.20 per share; the earnings release says the tender was substantially undersubscribed. It then bought approximately 0.7 million additional shares at an average price of $1.63, for a total of approximately 6.8 million shares, which the company describes as an approximately 7% reduction in shares outstanding. FY25 share repurchases were $9.1M. Buying back stock well below today's price was good for remaining holders. The counter-point is that ongoing stock-based compensation from pre-IPO RSUs offsets part of that reduction over time, and the release does not say whether further buybacks are planned.
management.governance: Per the proxy statement filed April 10, 2026, the Executive Committee, acting for the Board, determined that Mr. Christen, Ms. Liu and Ms. Pao are independent directors under Exchange Act and Nasdaq rules; the excerpt does not state the total board size. The Executive Committee also handles director nominations, and the company has no formal board diversity policy. All LT10 and LT50 shares are held by the Expensify Voting Trust, which holds 83.6% of voting power as of March 27, 2026, under an agreement intended to keep decision-making centered on employees. For outside Class A holders, this means they cannot change the board or block strategy; their protection rests on management's own economic alignment rather than on voting rights. The proxy also discloses employment arrangements with Mr. Alvarez Divo, Mr. Mills and Mr. Vidal as related-party transactions, including $1,650,985.94 of cash compensation to Mr. Mills as Chief Product Officer from January 1, 2025 through March 31, 2026.
management.insiderOwnership: As of March 27, 2026, per the proxy, David Barrett held 3.1% of Class A shares and 36.7% of voting power, and all current executive officers and directors as a group (8 persons) held 5.7% of Class A shares and 48.9% of voting power. Outside holders of more than five percent of Class A include Steve McLaughlin at 11.2% and Octopus Head Inc. at 7.3%. Insiders' economic stake in Class A is modest relative to their voting control, which is the main governance tension for outside holders.

idiosyncratic: Classic attrition: the CEO describes Classic as a pool that will naturally drain, and paid members fell 2% in Q2'26. If New Expensify does not grow faster than Classic shrinks, revenue keeps declining.

Card economics: per the 10-Q MD&A, rising Expensify Card adoption increases cashback contra revenue, which was a driver of the Q2 revenue decline, and the Visa volume incentives that offset cost of revenue fell in the quarter.

Contract terms: the 10-Q MD&A says arrangements are either month-to-month, terminable by either party without penalty, or annual with a minimum member count, so revenue can fall quickly if customers leave.
Partner dependence: the card program runs under an agreement with The Bancorp Bank, N.A. on the Visa network, so changes to that arrangement would affect interchange revenue.
Result volatility: the FY25 10-K risk factors (filed February 26, 2026) warn that quarterly and annual results have fluctuated significantly and may not meet investor or analyst expectations.
risks.systemic: The 10-Q MD&A says the business depends on the economy because the majority of customers are small and medium-sized businesses, and cites elevated inflation, tariff and trade issues, and geopolitical uncertainty including the conflict in the Middle East. Because revenue is billed on active members and card spend, a slowdown in hiring or business travel would show up quickly. The FY25 10-K risk factors (filed February 26, 2026) separately list declines in foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar as a source of fluctuation in results.

body: We rate Expensify HOLD with a $2.00–$2.80 target range. The free cash flow guidance and the Q2 buyback support the shares, and the scenario weighting in Valuation lands close to the current price. What would move us to BUY is evidence in reported revenue that New Expensify is outgrowing the Classic decline; what would move us to SELL is a free cash flow miss against the fiscal 2026 guide, which would remove the floor under the stock.
